utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'd now like to read a summary of Mr. Baraybar's testimony from the Krstic case. Mr. Baraybar testified in the Krstic case about the anthropological examination of human remains that were exhumed from Srebrenica-related graves between 1996 and 1999. He describes the following methodology that he used to determine the gender, the age, and the minimum number of individuals exhumed from those sites. First he would determine the gender of an individual. If this could not be determined by an examination of the external genitalia, it was done by examining the pelvic bone, the skull, and the long bones, in that order. Second, he would establish the age-range of each individual by examining changes in certain bones by using the so-called Suchey-Brooks method and relying on Bosnian population-specific standards. The relevant age-ranges were 8 to 12, 13 to 24, and over 25 years of age. Third, the minimum number of individuals at the site in question would then be calculated. This was done by adding together the total of the most commonly occurring bone in each age-range. Only a unique bone or one of a pair of bones would be used for this calculation. For example, if there were 38 left proximal femurs in the 13 to 24 age-range and 48 right proximal tibia in the 25 and over age-range, that would give a minimum number of 86 individuals for that particular site. To avoid overcounting, the human remains from a primary grave and any known secondary sites were examined together using the same bone as the basis of the calculations. Mr. Baraybar concluded that between 1996 and 1999 a minimum number of 1.883 individuals had been exhumed by the ICTY from Srebrenica-related graves. Of those 1.883 individuals, 1.656 were male, one was female, and 212 were of indeterminate sex. 1.547 of these individuals were aged 25 years or over at their time of death. Mr. Baraybar also testified that in 1999 he supervised the exhumation of mass graves at Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and the site known as Glogova 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Baraybar, I have a few additional questions for you. First, can you briefly describe to us what the procedure was once a body or a body part had arrived at the morgue.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Certainly, the -- all the remains that arrived to the morgue were placed in a refrigerated unit or container. Once a body would be taken out of the container, in a body bag, it would be logged in as being assigned to a specific autopsy table and pathologist team, meaning a pathologist, an anthropologist, a seen-of-crime officer, an autopsy technician. The body bag would be taken to a fluoroscope. A fluoroscope is an X-ray machine that allows you to scan through, with X-rays, the body bag looking for metal particles such as bullets. In some other occasions it became quite useful because we found, not in this case specifically but in other cases, live grenades with the bodies and things of that kind that could be very dangerous. After that, the body bag would be placed on the table, open. Pictures would be taken. The body placed on the table, undressed. All items of clothing, personal effects, and other associate artefacts would be given to scene-of-crime officer to describe them, log them, and take pictures of them. And the autopsy as such would progress. I mean, if it was a flesh body, opening the three cavities. If it was a skeletonised body, cleaning the bones, laying them out in anatomical position and then reconstructing broken parts to assess trauma. Obviously, in this process I mean age, sex, stature, and other characteristic would be recorded by anthropologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Were there times where you were involved in the reconstruction of broken parts of bones?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. What was your role as the chief forensic anthropologist?

Otherwise, it would be quite complicated to try to merge all the information from different people. To choose and discuss with my colleagues, as well, the best techniques that would be used to establish, for example, age or sex or stature. So primarily ensuring consistency, I would say, among all those that were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, can you briefly explain to the Court a little bit about the age-ranges that you used to calculate the minimum number of individuals. Why those three age-ranges? Why not use a greater number of more precise age-ranges?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The problem -- the problem we faced in this case was the large number of cases we were dealing with or large number of individuals that were involved in these calculations. So while every single set of remains was -- had a specific age determination depending on the number of elements available to be aged, in order to present the data in a comprehensible manner we have to include those individual estimates. For example, somebody being 18, 25, 27, or whatever other age, into broader age-ranges in order to present the data in an easier way. That is one part of the explanation. The second one is that a number of remains were fragmentary. So, for example, you may receive as a case a hand, a foot, a piece of a torso or a piece of a spine, a piece of a leg, and those elements did not yield much features in order for you to determine age in a precise manner. And I'm using the word "precision" and accuracy, meaning that precision is how -- how close you are in terms of the deviation from the real age. For example, I would say you could be -- you have a mean of 35 years of age plus/minus 2. I'm being very precise. But obviously I could be more accurate to say that you are between 20 and 50 years of age. Or 0 to a hundred. I would always be right and accurate, therefore. So the age-ranges only reflect a way to present data more than to establish individual age. I do not know whether I'm answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, I -- in a nutshell, the broader the age-ranges, the more accurately you're able to place individuals within those ranges.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is correct. Otherwise, if I try to be precise without having enough elements to support my age determination, I would be, I mean, doing it wrong. That's the bottom line of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR

Therefore, the remains in Hodzici come from Lazete, so we have merged them, because it is the same site, the same people pretty much. Is 243. And in Lazete 1 that is also related to the secondary sites of Hodzici Road 3 and 4 is 250. That's the MNI, the total minimum number of individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This report introduces a new phrase, the minimum minimal number of individuals exhumed by the ICTY forensic teams. Can you briefly explain the difference between MNI, or minimum number of individuals, and this new term MMNI?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The new term was coined in order not to cause, I mean, further confusion since the Chamber has seen many reports actually referring to minimal number of individuals. And this was yet again another merging exercise and would cause much confusion. The two words are clarifying two things: First, what the MNI is. And then we move on to the MMNI. The minimum number of individuals is a calculation, a very conservative calculation to explain at least how many people are represented by the bodies or body parts recovered in a grave-site. For example, if we had a grave with complete bodies, you would do a head count. I mean, you would just count them and that's it. But if you got complete people and pieces of people, then you would need to take another kind of decision and that is you cannot just simply count every piece as being one person because you could be wrong. We got two arms and two legs and you do not know whether a right and a left may go together from one person, so you cannot count them twice. What you need to do is to count either a bone or a part of a bone that is unique or one of a pair, for example the head or, for example, the right leg or the left leg and so on. In this way, you will determine at least how many people there are there. Not at most, but at least. And if you have individuals of another age, for example, you have right legs representing 25 adults but you may have an arm from a -- for a child, this arm is counting as one because an individual of a different age, they cannot be considered as part of the leg. So up to there, fine. Now we move to the minimal minimum. I'll try to explain this in the most clear way because it is quite complicated. At the beginning, we had primary sites, okay? Bodies were buried in a primary site. But these bodies were taken off the primary site and then buried in a number of secondary sites. Once it was established through a number of means, and I presume the Prosecution had already shared with the Court a number of these studies, that primary sites were related to a number of secondary sites, we had to merge in terms of numbers the remains found in the primary site and the secondary site, because they were part of the same thing, okay? But now, how can we get an estimate of all the bodies that ICTY recovered until the year 2000 so? We could not simply add the MNI for each site, because it will be yet again an overrepresentation. So we have to be even more conservative. And that's it. I give you an example. For the Glogova site, we used the right leg and for some other site we used the left leg. How do I know that these rights and the lefts are not together. So in order to do that, we have to normalise everything and use the same bone throughout all the sites, meaning that there were sites that were represented or further represented by other bones that were not counted, and that is why our estimate as the MMNI is -- that is the most, I mean, hyper conservative estimate we can get is 2.691 or 2.541. If we had counted simply all these MNIs I told you about, we would have got 2.691, okay? But our estimate that is the most conservative one is 2.541. That is the very, very least of how many people may have been represented by all the remains collected by ICTY until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Perhaps this will be -- to simplify it, we'll work through an example together. If you had ten graves, each of which had a minimum number of individuals of 50, now, the first nine graves used the left femur to calculate their MNI, but the tenth grave used the right femur. Now, when you add all of them up, the MNI is 500; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But because the MMNI only counts the most common bone across all graves, you don't count any of the right femurs from grave 10, but you do look at grave 10 to see if it contained any left femurs that you can add in to the total, so ... is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So say the tenth grave has 50 right femurs but it also has 25 left femurs, what will your MMNI be from those ten sites?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, you would just count -- you would just count the 25, not -- not -- not the 50. So it would be 475 rather than 500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one final question on a different topic. Can you explain --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Just -- what would you do, Doctor, with the remaining 25?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They exist, but you do not take them into account in your calculation because you try to be conservative. Meaning, you try to say, At the very least we got so many people. We most likely have more, but I cannot say for sure based on this calculation. In other words, it would be easier but less scientific, I would say, or serious, for that matter, to just simply count. Because it would be even easier to just count all the bodies parts we have and say, We've got 5.000 people there, but that is not true. So we have to say, At least, at the very, very, very least, we have so many people. So in order to be fair and very conservative, I'm going to use the same bone across the spectrum. Even if I know that 25 other people may be represented there, and I'm not counting them, but just -- it's a way to be very transparent with that and very conservative for the estimation. Because normally what actually happen is that they may tell you, You've been overcounting. You've been too generous in counting. So in order not to be told that, we're just, I mean, drawing back and saying we've got to be very conservative in counting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I can just add one other question to that, Mr. Baraybar. The reason why the right femur can't be counted in that scenario is because it may match a left femur; is that right? It may come from the same person?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Just a last question. Can you explain whether the anthropological analysis of remains and the anthropological calculation of MNI and MMNI is still relevant in light of advances in DNA technology?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That's a quite relevant question. Remember that DNA, as many other techniques, are complementary techniques. So you will need to start always with your MNI prior to deciding what technique to use to advance further. Because, having a preliminary number of people, then you can start with your testing to corroborate that. But what is very important to say is that DNA will always give you a much higher estimate than the MNI, because the MNI is that, it's a minimum number of individuals. I mean, DNA will allow you then to match, for example, right and left and say that perhaps you've got other individuals represented by other bones not counted in the MNI.

utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. I have no further questions.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Baraybar, good morning. First of all, I would like to thank you for meeting with the Defence. I hope that this will help us to proceed in a simple and efficient way. First of all, I wanted to ask you this: You worked --

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Certainly. As I said before, I really explained what I did in the morgue with the team of anthropologists that worked under my supervision. I participated in -- in the autopsies when I was in the area reconstructing body parts, doing determination of age, sex, stature, normal analysis in the morgue. And in the field I directed in some -- in some cases exhumations of some sites, as is indicated in my reports as well, with a team of archaeologists, surveyors, scene-of-crime officers, and those kind of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to be looking at a few of your documents simultaneously grouped by topics because we don't have time to test each document separately. In the report P4033, in the summary of the findings, you say that during your work you specialised --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is page 3, I think, in the report. 194 is the last ERN number. It's the summary of the finding. I'm afraid that that's not the number. Isn't the Eastern Bosnia one that got the number 4033? No, no, no. Not Glogova 2. Then it's the one dated the 8th of December, 1999, mass grave-sites in Eastern Bosnia. I made a mistake, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here you said that during the work of the specialists in the second half of 1989 in Eastern Bosnia three main localities were examined, Nova Kasaba, Konjevic Polje, and Glogova. Each one had graves where allegedly there were the remains of victims from the protected area of Srebrenica. Who said that these were the victims from those localities? Who said that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: As you -- as you perhaps know, as part of the OTP, or the Office of the Prosecutor, for which I was working, we knew we were working in the investigation of the -- on the fall of Srebrenica. However, I have indicated in the report that these were alleged victims, since that is information we had received. I have not affirmed in the first paragraph of this that they were victims from there because this information, the background information, we got. Certainly we got background information as to what investigation we're working on. So as far as that, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Baraybar. That's quite fair. So you did not establish that, but you -- you quoted that. Did the Prosecution inform you about the fact that that area was a front during the 42-month period of the civil war, where the fighting was constant during that period in that location?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I do not recall the Prosecution telling me that, but, I mean, I read that in some, I mean, background books I may have read at the time. But, I mean, nobody, let's say, informed me or gave me any formal report or information regarding where people may be placed or how the fighting was going on. I mean, remember, I'm a forensic, I mean, person, not a military analyst. So that information was not privy to me in any official form, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Does that mean that you were also not informed that you could encounter bodies from different time periods or from -- or bodies whose time of death was different?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, I mean, there was no information pertaining to what we would expect to find. We were primarily presented with a problem, so to speak, I mean, a number of potential graves, and to determine whether these were graves or not, to extract their contents in a scientific manner, and to make expert opinions based on our findings. So I don't think the issue was at any point in time that we were supposed to find something or the other. I mean, nobody ever told me what I was supposed to find. I mean, if that is what you're implying.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So it was not given to you as an assignment to differentiate between victims who fell before the 14th of July, 1995, and those who died during that week of the 14th of July. Do you know anyone else who was given that assignment, to make a distinction between those who died before the 13th of July, 1995, and who was killed in that critical week?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I mean, I'm not privy to any information pertaining to that. But as a matter of clarification, do remember that this was a forensic investigation. And in any forensic investigation you do not distinguish between types, let's say, of victims or qualify the remains you are finding as being victims of one kind or the other. You're collecting or recovering the scene as presented to you. So if you have a grave with 50 people inside, you will not be choosing, you know, 25 from this period and 25 from the other. You would just collect the scene as it is and then process the whole scene as it is. Certainly afterwards, I mean, definitely -- I mean, prosecutors, defence lawyers, will decide whatever they need for what. But, I mean, forensic personnel will be primarily recovering the seen and making, obviously, interpretations based on the findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In this same summary you also said that there were ten graves with at least 208 individuals recovered from them and it was established that 184 were determined as males, 1 was a female, and so on and so forth. When we're talking about these 76 persons aged between 13 and 24, do you agree that for legal and judicial purposes it is quite important to establish more precisely the facts and that this range from 13 to 24 is quite a large range?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Most definitely. However, as I said yet again at the beginning, this is the way we are reporting a large number of cases. Not -- this doesn't mean that every single case has the same age-range. Meaning, if we go back to the autopsy reports of every single case, you will have a specific, I mean, age determination for each of them. Okay? So, for example, you may have somebody between 13 and 16. That would be included in the range 13 to 24, but that doesn't mean that the individual age estimation for each of them is a range. The range is just a way to present information. And also remember that when you estimate age in bones, you will always give a range. And that's the whole thing of precision and accuracy. Meaning, you could say, oh, this person looks like 16, but it is most likely that this person is between, let's say, 14 and 18, because you cannot say by examining the bones that this person had 16.2 years. I mean, that -- I mean, you cannot do that. That's chronological age. You're establishing only biological age. But to answer your question, the specific age estimate would be found in the autopsy report of that specific case. This is just a way of reporting. So not to, kind of, confuse the two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just ask for your understanding. I am asking this because the Prosecution generally characterizes the victims by saying that 8.000 Muslim or Bosniak males and young boys were killed. So the Defence has to clarify what young boys, what that term signifies. So we have not yet come to the specific description of what is a young boy. But in your report what I would like to know is that I can see that -- well, you didn't do that yourself, others did that, the anthropological examination of the bodies. Let's look at the ERN number 107. This is the last page, the age indicators. How did it happen that we have the interval from 8 to 12, then from 13 to 17, and then from 15 to 24, age-ranges? This overlap, does that not allow for the possibility of some remains being counted in two groups?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see that page as well, Mr. Karadzic? If you could be of assistance, Doctor, as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that that is 4033, exhibit, but I'm not quite sure that that is that exhibit. But we're talking about the anthropological examination, in any event, so then that would be -- I think that that's on page 7, I would say. The title of that report is the "Report on the Anthropology Examination of Human Remains." The number is P4030.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I have it in front of me. As I told you before, because individual remains or sets of remains have individual age estimates, it was a matter of fitting those individual age estimates into some intervals, because otherwise, for example, in the example you refer before of the 76 cases, I'm going to refer to the individual estimate for each of the 76, and it would take obviously --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one, Doctor.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here we see this table, and that's what I would like to discuss. Please go on, Doctor, but please bear in mind that I would like you to focus on this portion alone, the age-ranges which are not clearly defined statistically, and it is possible that some of the remains actually belong to a number of groups, not just one.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. However, there's bound to be overlap between certain age categories, primarily regarding young -- young people. The overlap will generally happen -- generally happen between the younger people. Why is this? We have been using here indicators of a growth of bones and the development of teeth. Okay? And obviously sometimes in many people, and due also to specify circumstances, for example, if people are malnourished and all the rest of it, they will grow less and develop and continue developing. So, for example, the teeth can give you an age and the bones can give you another age. Okay? That is, that the person will be older because of the teeth and will be younger because of the -- of the long bones. Of course, yes, there is an overlap, but we're not talking an overlap of ten years. You're talking an overlap of six months or maybe a year. Okay? This retardation of growth will happen in that way. And, yes, there is a possibility of people being fitted into an interval to which they do not belong. If we were keeping these very rigid intervals as I pointed here, like 8 to 12, and 13, et cetera. That's why we merged the things of the 15 to 24, because it would be yet again a more conservative way of putting, let's say, younger or several people together, okay, in the teens, rather than dividing the teens. But whenever you have a problem of overlap, it is likely that it will be towards the young side, not towards the older side. So misclassification in this case may happen that you may confuse people as being older but as a matter of fact are younger. I don't know whether I am answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Baraybar. Now, who was it who decided that they should be merged?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Oh, I decided that. I decided that for -- for reporting -- yet again for reporting purposes. Yet again, as I said before, these were reporting -- it's a way of reporting large number of cases. I mean, if we -- we had five cases or ten cases, of course we would say, you know, individual one has this age, and two, and so forth. But in this case you're talking about, I mean, hundreds, I mean, a few thousand in this case. So it would be, I mean, absurd to refer to the specific or individual age estimated for each person. In that case we would need to bring every case and read every single case, you know, one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I do see that there were scientific and anthropological reasons for that. However, for forensic purposes would you agree that the Defence especially has a vested interest in establishing more precisely the presence of minors in the -- in this population of victims?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I mean, most definitely. But then we could go back -- I can -- I can give you an explanation for that, and something even that the Defence may want to do. If we look at -- and I don't know how to tell you to look for this, but I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could read out the title of your report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The title, certainly. If we go to the calculation of the minimal number of individuals of the report from January 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's Exhibit P4037. Page 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We go to page 8 of that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this it, Mr. Baraybar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For example, here we were using the old -- again, we're going back to the old separation of age-ranges. The Defence, for example, would like to examine, perhaps, the autopsy reports of the specific cases listed here that could be minors or younger people, and you see that in the category 8 to 12 you have seven people. So in principle you could review the autopsy reports of these seven people and find out why they were placed in that age-range. What you will likely find is that the teeth had a level of development as that age or that the bones were not fused, certain bones were not fused, or that, for example, the pelvic bone was separated, still not fused, and therefore these people are likely to be minors. You could also examine in detail perhaps this 157 autopsy reports of these people from 13 to 17 and see whether they will be -- they will qualify as people under 18, or minors, and so forth. All I'm trying to say is that we should not confuse the way things are reported and believe that because they are reported in that way the individual autopsy reports also follow the same, let's say, vagueness, if we can use that term. I mean, this way of reporting is only to simplify the presentation of a very large number of cases. But it is always possible to go back to the specific autopsy report and look at the anthropology form and say, Okay, how did I establish age in this specific individual? And you will have an estimate, an age estimate for that specific case that would be fitted into that age category, but it would have its own estimate based on specific evidence. So my advice for you would be to review, perhaps, these -- these cases and to get to the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be reasonable to expect, though, that up until the age of 25, based on the fusing of the bone ends and the cartilage and bone connections, it would be possible to determine more precisely the age, with an error of probably plus or minus one year?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, not plus/minus one year. Remember that the 25 cutting point is primarily given by the partial or complete fusion of the -- the medial epiphysis of the clavicle. There is a number of epiphyses or the ends of long bones that by then already are closed. So, kind of, the last bony piece that is in this case to fuse is the medial clavicle and that is why we're using it as a cut-off point. As a matter of fact, most of the epiphyses are already fused much earlier than that, you know, by 17, by 18, and there is a variation among individuals. And actually females, even by 16 they could be already closed. So, no. As a matter of fact, no. And you could use teeth, perhaps, to get something much more precise, like a year plus/minus, but not a long bone or any bone epiphysis fusion, never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, is it possible to see a concrete autopsy report to see how the age is reflected in it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'll find one. And if you can give me a couple of minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.text: Or we can do that after the break.

utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. And just one further question in order to be clear, Mr. Baraybar. You see this table, so the second and third category overlaps in terms of age. First one -- second one being 13 to 17, and third one, 15 to 24. So there's overlap of as far -- overlap as far as age 15, 16, 17 are concerned. But in terms of counting, there should be no overlap because they are based upon each autopsy report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And also, Your Honour, remember that you're counting specific bones. Perhaps for Mr. Karadzic, and for the Chamber as well, to -- just for an issue of clarification, the -- the way in which we grow and we mature is not really linear. So you cannot really say this person is 16 and this person is 15, because there are 15-year-olds that look like 18 and 18 that look like 13 perhaps, and so on and so forth. So it's not really a -- there's always an overlap. So it is not -- let's put it, it is an exact science but it's not a precise science. It is an accurate science but not really precise in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we can now just revisit the earlier document P4030, please. You mentioned today, and I also found it somewhere in your reports, that the undernourishment and lifestyle and so on can affect the precision in determining one's age; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: What I meant is that, to give you an example, malnourishment, disease, and so on, even high altitude, for that matter, would affect the balance between growth and development. So generally growth is sacrificed for development. So, for example, somebody -- not to say malnourished, but someone in high altitude, like in my part of the world, that lives at 4.500 metres above sea level will be smaller people. Fully developed, but smaller. Meaning that the body in a way chooses to develop fully, sacrificing growth. So for example, if you were to measure the bone of a child in that respect and compare it to a European child, you would say, Okay, this child is, I mean, younger because the bone is smaller. But it doesn't mean that he's younger, he's just simply smaller. So you've got these issues. But when you compare and you use, for example, the teeth and the bone together, you get a very good estimate. If you get only one of the two, you may be underestimating age. But yet again, as I told you, it is not a matter of many years. You're not talking about -- by saying, This person I think is 5, and suddenly he's 15, that is not -- I mean, the variation is much smaller than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you want to look at an autopsy report right now --

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it could be easier if we get a printout so that my associate Professor Dunjic could also take a look at it during the break and then perhaps it will be easier to proceed. And perhaps we can also obtain a Serb -- a B/C/S version, Serbian version.

utterances.text: So --

utterances.text: Let's -- let's do it later on. Yes, later on. I'll leave it in the parties -- leave it in the hands of the parties. Let's proceed. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have P4030 on the screens again, page 6, please. That's the paragraph or, rather, the chapter on age.

utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now we have it. Now, I am a bit puzzled by something here. It is clear, namely, that the sternal range of the fourth rib and then pubic symphysis, that two is clear. However, the sentence, the above-mentioned techniques in determining the age was obtained by the standards for epiphysical [as interpreted] union as described by Simmons and Web and Suchey, and so on, for the Bosnian population, so would that mean that they actually established certain anthropological specificities or racial, if you will, for the Bosnian individuals and did they actually differentiate, distinguish between Serbs, Croats, and Bosniaks? In other words, the reliance here on the Simmons work, could you tell us a bit about it? What is it that they did?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Okay. Let me put this into context first to be understood by everybody. We used -- for aging adults, we're no longer talking about bones fusing or teeth growing or anything of the kind for people over 25. Two techniques that are known to be very robust techniques, these techniques, called the Suchey-Brooks and the Iscan and Loth, look at some changes in the pubic symphysis, that is, the anterior part of the hip bone, and the end of the rib of the fourth rib close to the cartilage that joins from the sternum. These parts of the bone do change with age. They were original developed, I mean, the technique, that is, a technique of phases, from 1 to 6 or 1 to 8 or whatever, they change with age, and they were developed originally in the United States. Okay? The Suchey-Brooks techniques was developed using an autopsy room sample from Los Angeles with a multi-racial sample of over 700 people, while the Iscan and Loth was a sample for Caucasians and African Americans from Florida. Okay? Simmons and Associates did a correction of the age-ranges for each of the phases on an autopsy room sample from Tuzla. Okay? That is the closest sample that existed at the time for a Balkan population. And I'm not distinguishing here whether, you know, it is similar or different to -- or is a difference between Croatians and Serbs and whoever else. I mean, it's just for the area. Such as, for example, the sample that used Suchey-Brooks was a sample from Los Angeles. So what I'm saying for Bosnian population, I mean for the Bosnia population leaving the territory of Bosnia that ended up in the mortuary in Tuzla. So I do not know if they determined the ethnicity of the cadaver that was being examined. But that is the closest data that existed at the time regarding a population-specific sample, you know? Because we were told as well at some point, Oh, you've been using standards derived from an American population. How does an American population has to do with the Balkans? Okay, well therefore the data was corrected now to a sample from the Balkans, irrespective of, let's say, ethnicity. When I say Bosnian population, because Tuzla, as far as I'm concerned, is in Bosnia, and, you know, whoever ended up in the morgue in Tuzla would be a Bosnian -- I'm not saying -- giving this with any ethnic connotations so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this method -- or, rather, this standard used by Simmons and others for Bosnia -- for the Bosnian population, is it -- has it been standardised and has it received scientific support or was it just a sample that was done by them? So was it scientifically confirmed that there are certain anthropological characteristics for people in Bosnia that are different from those of other people from other areas?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, I can give you more data regarding this. At the time, Simmons and Associates was the only standard that was being created. They did not apparently keep working on -- on this issue. However, this data was even slightly modified -- or, rather, perfected by another study based on a population sample from Kosovo in 2008, if I'm not mistaken, by Kimmerle and Associates. And when you compare the sample from Kosovo yet again as a sample from the Balkans - yet again I'm not differentiating here whether the people involved here could be Albanian or Serbs or -- or Romas or whatever - and you compared, for example, with a population sample from the US, yes, there are differences. And the overall difference would be - yet again I'm oversimplifying things, but I can give you certainly the references if you'd be interested - is that the Balkan samples when compared to the American samples in starting more or less on the fourth decade, they look older. In other words, if you have, I don't know, a pubic symphysis phase 4, for example, and this phase 4 would be, let's say, 40 years of age for the American sample, in the Balkans it would be 45. So if we were using American standards at the time, we would be underaging people that would be actually older. By that is for adults, not for younger people. These are people 25 and plus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if it is convenient, we will take the break now. Mr. Baraybar, there is one administrative matter we'd like to deal with in your absence. So we will resume at 11.00. So you may be excused now. In the meantime, could the Chamber move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: A glance back at the transcript indicated there might be some confusion, if the Court looked at the transcript for next week's anticipated schedule. So to clarify: It should be Misters Groenewegen and Patelski on Wednesday and concluding with Professor Haglund on Thursday. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could we get the hard copy of these autopsy? Ah, sorry, sorry. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we've got three autopsy reports here from the Cancari 12 site that you saw the exhumation of yesterday. There's one from each of the three age ranges that Mr. Baraybar has talked about, and they're also relevant to the testimony of Dr. Lawrence who will be here next week, so we can discuss them again then. But I don't know if you'd like the witness to be shown one now or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those have been disclosed to the Defence, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I believe so, but we'll double-check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And why don't you hand over the hard copy for their convenience, and I'll leave it in the hands of Mr. Karadzic whether to put that to the witness or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. But before we continue, Judge Baird has a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Dr. Baraybar, just -- just a very brief question on the question of the samples. Can we assume that the Tuzla sample and the Kosovo sample harmonised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Roughly speaking, yes, they do. I mean, I do -- I was checking in the break the age-ranges per phase as I was telling you. I mean, you have, for example, for each of the techniques you can have a number phases and see what are the age brackets of each of them and they are more or less the same, but they are different to the American sample.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Baraybar, I'm a little nonplussed by these norms, by these standards applied. I'm looking at your document P4030 and the CV, and I can't find the Simmons or somebody else endeavoured to establish standards for the Bosnian man. But on the last page I see in one work that this paper was once presented at the American Academy for Forensic Medicine. This is the penultimate on your list, Simmons, Tuco, Kesetovic, and Cihlarz. But that a paper has been presented somewhere does not mean that the work itself has been accepted and that the norm has been established. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. As a matter of fact, no. Remember, for a paper to be accepted into the -- represented to the academy, it has to go in through peer review. I mean, it is not that you submit a paper and it gets automatically accepted. That's not the case. It is true, though, that the paper never made it into publication, and that is something that we should ask perhaps Simmons and Associates. It is true, however, that the nature of the investigation in terms of the raw data that I actually got from Simmons at that time is quite sound. It is quite sound. I don't see any problems with it. And as I said a moment ago, the results of Simmons are quite similar, I would say, although the technique is different in terms of statistics used to treat the data, from what Kimmerle and Associates did in 2008 that actually was published in the Journal of Forensic Sciences.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before this, something from the American journal for physical anthropology. Isn't there any more recent reference than this one where African Americans are referred to as Negroes? Isn't the term a bit obsolete? So isn't the paper itself obsolete? Hasn't there been any progress since 1952 in the field? It's almost 45 years now.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I believe it has, but I do not see the relationship of one thing with the other. I have not mentioned this. I have not mentioned the American Journal of Physical Anthropology in these references, although the technique I'm referring to of the Iscan and Loth technique from a sample of Caucasian and African Americans is not from the 1950s. It's much later than that. I mean, much, much later than that. So I do not, I mean, see the parallel between the two things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, has the same been done in Vietnam? Is that how comparisons were made such as between African Americans and whites in America? Was the same done in Vietnam, and was that standardised?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I do not understand, I mean, your question. What was standardised? Are you referring to a technique in particular, to the fourth rib in this case? Or what are you asking me about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, indexes for recalculation of age was standardised here. Was a similar index established for the Bosnian man, be it a Serb, Croat, or Muslim? Has that been scientifically approved, that it can be repeated in any scientific experiment and produce the same results? Has this recalculation been standardised?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, let me try to answer your question as I understand it. We have referred to two techniques here. One is changes in the pubic symphysis, that is this anterior part of the pelvis, and the other on the fourth rib. Okay? The techniques, meaning the observations of the changes in these bones, and the classification of these changes into phases was developed in the United States, one in a sample, a very large sample in Los Angeles, and the other one in a sample, smaller, in Florida. While these changes and the phases remain the same, okay, the composition of the population sample has changed, for example in the sample of Simmons or the sample of Kimmerle or some other samples in any other country in the world. So to that we call population-specific standards. Meaning, I will develop the same technique in a Peruvian population. So I will look at the same phases, but I may get to the conclusion that phase one in the US sample is, whatever, 20 years of age, and in Peru is 22 or 19 or something of the kind. So this thing that we would call calibration has been done, for example, for the Balkans by Simmons in 1999, in this paper you refer to, by Kimmerle in 2008 with this Kosovo sample, and is being done, as a matter of fact, in other places. I mean, most of the -- well, not most, but a number of people in the world use these techniques. They are very well established, they're very solid, very robust. Nobody will say that they're useless. Or the opposite; they're quite useable. And I would calibrate this according to the population. As a matter of fact, if I'm recalling now correctly, there is even a study in Serbia by Marija Djuric, published, perhaps, in Forensic Science International, isn't it? Professor Djuric - I'm just almost in a dialogue here - but, I mean, Marija Djuric did a study on this. So what I'm trying to say -- and she's a Serbian forensic doctor. So what I'm saying is it is a very useful technique and therefore investigators throughout the world tend to calibrate - that would be the proper word - these techniques to their own population standards. So the answer would be yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And reckoning with the papers of Kesetovic and Cihlarz, that implies a certain reference group, a certain reference value. Do you know what that control group was for them?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I may or may not have the specific sample sizes they used. Let me check on my notes. Oh, I do. So, for example, the male sample with 242 individuals and the females was actually quite small with 52, and that is for the pubic symphysis. And for the ribs they used 233 males and 52 females as well. Obviously compared, for example, to the -- to the Suchey-Brooks sample, it is smaller, but statistically significant nevertheless. I mean, Suchey-Brooks has 739 cases, so it is like a third. But it's still, I mean, a fairly large sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I understand, Dr. Baraybar, but in order to establish an index for conversion for a specific population such as the Bosnian one, there must be a reference value. A control group has to exist. Did Cihlarz and Kesetovic provide evidence of this? Because any statement made in the academy has to be verifiable.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes, but let's just clarify. And maybe we're missing something here in the translation. It is not an index for conversion. It is really a calibration, so to speak. And I explain you how it works. It is actually much more simple -- I mean, simple than what it sounds. So imagine the following: The advantage of working with an autopsy room sample is that you get individuals who come in with a chronological age, an identity, so you know this person is -- the age is stated in ID card or something of the kind. So that is your control group. You're starting with a control group based on the identity of the person in that case and on the age of the person in that specific case. So that is a control group in itself. You study from the known. Okay? So when I say you got 242 people, you got 242 people that had chronological age and were identified, or meaning they were identified and therefore they have an age. So that is your control group. You do not need, let's say, a holdout sample that comes from somewhere else. I mean, it is -- your control group is the one that you base in your examination. So you say, Okay, I got 242 people. Divided by a decade, for example. You could -- the one between 10, 20, and 30; 30 and 40; and so on. So you're going to look at this bone piece and you say, Okay, irrespective of the age of the person, I would ascribe this fragment to phase 2. Okay? So then you will count all your phases 2 and you say, Okay, the phase 2 I got people that are 20, 22, 25, 30; therefore, your range is between 20 and 30. That's a super-simplification of the -- of the issue. That's the way you would actually do it. So it is sound. Yes, it is sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, but in these ranges that you mention it cannot be more precise, can it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Oh, most definitely not, because you're trying to be accurate more than precise. Remember that establishing the age of adults, I mean, people over 25 that have all their bits and pieces -- I mean -- I mean, fused, looking at the bones is very imprecise, I mean, unprecise. It is quite accurate but unprecise. I mean, you well know that is individuals that are -- that look much older what they are or younger than what they are. So, for example, if I give you a very popular example why a soccer player retires at age 35, because the knees most likely will be totally destroyed by activity, meaning playing soccer. So if you're looking at the bones of such a person and, you see, looking at the knees, you have only the legs, you say, Oh, this person is very old, because the knees are totally destroyed. And they happen to be 35, not 85. So it is definitely -- what you have at hand is much less than what you have when the people are younger, where the teeth are developing and the bones are getting fused or growing. So, yes, you are unprecise but more accurate. Let's put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now on page 103 of this document, the previous page, and you stated there very correctly that these are alleged victims from the Srebrenica area, the protected area, victims who were killed in 1995. The aerial photographs of moved earth, et cetera, was that the key indicator where you need to dig?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I would say that it was more an orientation, and it varied according to the site. So, for example, if I would give you a practical example, what you see from above is that the -- that the earth has been scraped. So you got, like, a stain, so to speak, of soil, that what you see from above. So from above you're not really seeing, not always, at least, that you have a grave. So you have to actually determine whether this big stain of soil corresponds to one grave, two graves, many graves, or where the grave is located. I mean, based on that it's just an orientation. It's not, you know, a specific thing. There are other sites where this stain is smaller perhaps and then you can, kind of, focus more in an area. But there are some other areas, and I'm thinking specifically on the Glogova site, where you have this enormous stain and the grave obviously was like all over under this stain. So it's just a reference. I mean, it's just only a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you assist us somehow in obtaining daily changes of the appearance of the ground, because from the 5th to the 25th of August is too long a period, and again very imprecise, because we have a phase of unlawful killing and executions on the one hand and we have the phase of burial of those killed in the woods. Do you know what it looked like on the 15th, the 16th, the 17th of July, or did you take as reference points only the 5th and the 25th?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: It would be for me impossible to know how the ground look at any point in time. I mean, your previous question referred to what I saw on the aerial photograph that I was shown, and obviously I only know what I saw on those photographs and on the days or the dates marked on those photographs. I wouldn't have any means of knowing how it looked or how the ground looked from above in those dates. But as I told you, the photograph, for me, was simply a reference. And it's very important to say this because some -- some of the -- of the sites did not necessarily -- there was not a hundred per cent correspondence between the stain you saw and -- say that you have a stain and the site would be, I don't know, right in the middle under it. Could be a bit on the side. I mean, the way -- little variations regarding the way you see it from above and the way you find it on the ground. So the answer is no. I mean, there's no way for me to know how the ground looked in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then we'll approach the Prosecution to try to obtain daily photographs. And when you say killed in 1995 in Eastern Bosnia-Herzegovina, were you expected to distinguish or did anyone else distinguish between those who were possibly unlawfully killed and those who were killed in combat, the combat that lasted all of that month? Because they must have been buried somewhere too.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. I think that this relates to a previous question you asked at the beginning of this examination. As I said, all these references are just references to the information I was privy to. I mean, I am not in a position, nor I was then, to -- based on my own observations, so to speak, to determine the nature of -- of people being buried there, meaning the way combatants, noncombatants. Obviously all the interpretations that are presented in these reports are based on the analysis or after the analysis of the evidence was recovered from the sites we were indicated to recover. As I said, we were not told at any point in time, Go and exhume that grave because that grave contains so-and-so and so. Obviously that was not the type of information we received. All the background information we received is that yes, this area contain the casualties or the victims of -- or alleged victims of the fall of Srebrenica, but that is just background information we obviously needed to proceed with our work. But not further than that. We never got any type of, I don't know, specific instruction or information regarding the nature, specific nature, of the victims we were dealing with. And obviously, and it's also present in the report, most of the statements I have written down here are based on direct observations of things. So, for example, I would find a body that was dressed. And in a preliminary examination of the remains, you could see it has a wallet in the pocket. And then you would open the wallet and you would find an ID card with a name and that would be a cursory thing at that moment because that will be very helpful for the mortuary, to, for example, open the ICRC, the International Committee for the Red Cross, book of the missing and find the name of Mr. So-and-so that was the name matching in the ID card, and according to this report this person was last seen in the enclave of Srebrenica in July 1995, and therefore that information would be written down in the report. Nothing more than that that you have seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. With all due respect, Dr. Baraybar, my first question today related to those killed before July 1995. However, do you agree that even within the number of those killed in July 1995 for the purposes of this Court it was necessary to make a distinction between those killed unlawfully and those killed in combat? So before July 1995, or between -- before 13 July 1995, it's one batch of people, and in July is another batch. Was your team able to distinguish between those two or even three categories?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I think the answer to this question has two parts. The first part, and this is the straight answer, that would be no. But the second part will be however - because there's an explanation that complements this no - obviously through a naked-eye examination of a cadaver, of a body, be it decomposed, preserved, or not, you will not be able to say when this person died, let's say, in 1992, 1993, 1994, 1995, obviously not. However, the associate elements or evidence to those bodies are the ones that make us think and infer, therefore, that these people were likely killed in such and such date. This association - and, as a matter of fact, association is one of the principles of archaeological practice, be it forensic or otherwise - it would allow us to infer, for example, that if I find a body that is dressed, that has personal effects on it, among which is an ID card and the name on that ID card that belongs to a male with a given name appears, for example, in the book of the missing of the ICRC as being seen last in the enclave of Srebrenica in 1995, a priori and unless is proven otherwise my logical inference would be that this person indeed died after July 1995, after this person was last seen. Obviously if, for example, I was able to demonstrate - and to my knowledge that is not the case until now - that this person was not the person bearing the ID card, that would be something different. You know, happened to be somebody who died three years before. That's -- that's a possibility. But as I told you, everything is possible, but not everything is probable. So they are two different things. I mean, possibility is 50/50 pretty much, but probability is something different. So it is very important to bear that in mind. So strictly speaking, obviously no. The answer is no, as I told you. But: No, but. And the "but" rebuts, in a way, the no, because it is not a matter of naked-eye observation of a body. Certainly, I mean, observing a cadaver like this, I mean, I cannot, I mean, tell you much more than that. I mean, did it die in year one or year three? Well, kind of difficult. I will not be able to tell you he did, unless I have some other associate evidence, that in this case I do have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You now mentioned clothing and such. Would you agree that in Glogova and in RV site, that is to say Ravnice, adult males were found wearing clothing such as camouflage trousers, soldiers' boots, et cetera? Was any conclusion drawn from that? Was it observed, noted, and was it then perhaps established that those were combatants?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Before you answer Mr. Baraybar. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Could I ask for a cite, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's from the findings of that entire team. It says this was found on these sites. I can find the reference later, but I thought perhaps the witness remembers that this clothing and gear was found on the bodies. We'll find the cite later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Can you answer the question, Mr. Baraybar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm looking at some of the reports because I don't want to rely only on memory, because as far as memory is concerned I personally do not recall, personally, that, finding somebody in military fatigues or with military gear. However, again, I do recall, and I have such occurrence here, for example, in the site of Glogova 5, finding a -- in grave A a loaded Beretta pistol, calibre 7.65 millimetres, in a leather holster associated to one of the bodies, that is, 152B, for example. But this person is not dressed in any -- dressed with any military fatigues. In one of the Nova Kasaba sites, I think there was also a number of rounds -- or live rounds of ammunition. But, yet again, not, as I said, associate to somebody dressed in military fatigues. So it would be a matter of then reviewing the specific cases, because, I mean, if it's based on my memory alone, I mean, I wouldn't -- I wouldn't trust it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Talking about the state of the mortal remains, the preservation of the corpse, you speak of that on the fifth page of the report. This is the report 4030. And you're talking about primary and secondary graves. Are these your findings or did you rely on Professor Wright's findings?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: A combination of the two. Because, remember that as much as -- well, not as much, actually less, than Professor Wright, because he devoted quite a lot of time at the exhumation of sites. I also directed a number exhumations, but I also participated, for periods, in some exhumations with Professor Wright. So it is a combined thing. As a quote, of course I'm quoting here Professor Wright's report, that would be the most appropriate thing to do, but it is a combined thing. So it is my personal observations but also I'm subscribing Professor Wright's testimony in that matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In view of the fact that for 42 months this was the front specially active until spring 1993, I'm interested in this finding regarding the integrity of the remains. You said that from an anthropological aspect the degree of fragmentation is one element, and the second is the saponification. Did you have any examples of mummification? Would a dry soil lead to skeletonisation or would you also encounter examples of mummification?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I do not recall example of mummification on the top of my head again, but remember that preservation is primarily related to the conditions of burial. So, for example, a -- a site that is well drained, that is -- that allows water to seep through it, so, for example, a kind of rocky -- more than rocky, a soil full of gravel would allow water to go through it and then this would tend primarily to allow or promote skeletonisation of bodies. As an example, if we can use examples to illustrate this, for example, the site found at the Brnice Dam that was dug into one of the dam platforms that was full of gravel, the bodies were skeletonised, were primarily just bones, while some other sites such as, for example, some of the -- which site? Some of the Nova Kasaba sites, for example, there was a clay-rich soil that tends to trap humidity. Bodies were saponified, meaning that the fat saturates and becomes a combination between wax -- I mean, a wax or a butter, as something quite hard. But as mummified bodies, I do not really recall. I recall some mummified bodies from other cases that has nothing to do with this one, but not really, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that judging by the integrity of the remains it -- actually, that is a very important element in determining the time of death, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Certainly. More than -- yeah. Integrity understood as preservation more than integrity, because integrity here is used in the term of the -- whether the body's complete or not. I mean, so I'm using the word integrity here more than -- to differentiate between complete bodies and incomplete bodies. Primarily in this last case, incomplete bodies due to the so-called robbing or tampering of grave-sites. But in general terms, yes, preservation is -- is -- is crucial, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I'm afraid I did not say integrity, "celovitost." I did say preservation or the degree of the degradation. So this is where the mix-up comes from. I said that I was talking about the degree of degradation or the degree of the changes in the body and that that is something that would indicate the time of death, would it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Up to a certain extent, yes. But remember the following: It is totally different to establish a post-mortem interval or the time since death in a cadaver, okay, where you can go for hours up to, let's say, days than after a certain time in which the body is buried and how it is preserved. What I'm trying to say is the following: Would you be able, by looking at -- at the naked eye, to a body to say that this body has been buried here for two months and three days or one year and one day? Of course you cannot. Yet again, we go back to the whole issue of precision and accuracy. If you do have a cadaver, certainly you can take temperature, you can look at rigor mortis, livor mortis, and another number of changes. But in this case, no. So what I'm trying to say with this is that preservation or -- preservation of the remains here was more dependent on the burial environment, okay, but this would not allow you in precise terms to make an estimate of a post-mortem interval with the same precision that you would do it with a cadaver. So, for example, it would be very difficult to say these people died, let's say, in 1995 or they died at the end of 1994 or -- well, not the end of 1994 but it would be winter, but they would die in 1994 or 1993 or so on, however - and that comes with however - we are not looking at bodies in a vacuum. They are not naked bodies in a hole. You have bodies with elements that are associated to them. And this means, yet again, another principle is that the context, in a way, defines up to a certain extent what your interpretations will be. Because you have bodies that are clothed, that have items of varies kinds that will give you a relative dating. Not an absolute dating. Absolute dating would be something like carbon 14 when you do a scientific test and will give you a specific number. In this case it would be relative. So ID card, name, found book of the missing July 1995, therefore, I mean, you've got already a relative dating in that -- in that respect. So your -- to answer your question, yes you're right in what you're saying, but, I mean, it cannot be taken out of context, regrettably. I mean, we are not just looking at bodies, I mean, naked bodies with no nothing found in a hole where you have less elements to make a determination. In this case you have to combine all these elements to make a logical inference.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And talking about days, what sort of precision would you be able to achieve if we're talking about the time period or the range in days?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Again, based on the naked observation of the bodies alone, none. However, you got some other materials that are associated like the watches. And I believe that you may have seen -- there's a report by Mr. Mills, who's a watch specialist, and you may also know that a number of automatic watches were found in various sites, primary, secondary, on somebody's wrist or about in the field or the field of the grave, and automatic watches, as far as I know, are operated by the oscillation of the wrist. And when -- when you stop -- I mean, when the wrists stop moving or oscillating, for example, when you're dead, it will take between 32 and 35 hours, if I'm not mistaken - I'm literally referring to another report that is not mine - for it to stop. And then the day and date combination found in those watches, the way -- throughout my report you're going to see a number of references for these watches, is always the same. It's Friday the 15th or Saturday the 15th, although there was no Saturday the 15th or Saturday the 16th in reality, so it's a little problem with the watch. But Friday the 15th are different times. If you subtract the number of hours, you get to the 13th. So yet again that would be another indirect element - forgetting about the book of the missing, forget about the ICRC and all the rest of it - to try to establish a time, you know, and a date interval for these individuals who have been placed in that -- in that grave. Now, is it scientifically sound? Totally scientifically sound. You're going to use whatever you have at hand that makes sense in order to make a logical inference. I mean -- and it's very practical. As a matter of fact, I consider that approach extremely practical. That was never used before. I mean, personally I didn't know much about automatic watches until Mr. Mills came out with his report, and I found it quite, I mean, quite interesting as a matter of fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And in your report you mentioned Friday the 15th, while Professor Wright 's report talks about Saturday the 15th. Perhaps this was then something that indicated two different months. Perhaps even years. For example, each month, if the date is different, if last month -- if Saturday was the 15th, the following month the 15th would be the Friday, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: You could be right. The problem is that, at least in as far as I'm concerned, and I have indicated that in my report, we found watches within the same grave that have these two day/dates combination. So the most likely explanation for this, considering -- taking all the context as a whole, is that is more a malfunction of the watch than something else. Let me clarify this. If I find bodies with ID cards of people that were last seen missing in Srebrenica, book of the missing of the ICRC, and the watches all together, okay, obviously the likelihood of this Saturday 15th being another year is highly unlikely. It is much more probably that it is a malfunction of the watch than a body was kind of inserted in -- I mean, no. It's just improbable. I mean, I won't say impossible, but it is improbable in this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Baraybar, I want to tell you why the Defence insists on this. For example, if you have a person who was seen for the last time in Srebrenica, let's say on the 9th, the 10th, or the 11th of July, and then the person was found in one of the graves, are you able to establish whether the person died or was killed on the 12th, 13th, the 14th, or the 15th, or the 16th, or after the 16th? Are you able to establish how long the body stayed on the ground, on the surface, before burial? In other words, as a forensics expert, are you able to provide my forensics experts with such a description of putrefactory changes which would seem reasonable and logical to him and that he could agree with?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, it is very difficult. And the reason why is that you are not talking about individual graves. So, okay, let's wind back for a -- I mean, rewind for a moment. The basic elements that were found in -- in many of the bodies, I wouldn't say all of the bodies, were a cadaverica fauna. So you got primarily fly larvae. As you know, the colonisation of flies to dead bodies is -- occurs very, very fast. And this was alledgedly, yet again, if we're talking about 1995, summertime. So it was quite hot, and flies don't take much long to lay their eggs on body orifices. I mean, it could be ears, nostrils, mouth, et cetera. Or open wounds, for that matter. So all I can say is that the bodies we found had at least colonisation of flies at the level of -- at the larval stage. And in -- you also know that a larvae can grow eating pretty much away flesh in various conditions as long as it is kind of warm, moist, et cetera. Even if the body has been, for example, buried. If the body has been buried, the larvae will continue being, kind of, alive and there they will go to a quiescent stage, and so on. So in that respect the interval of time for the position of eggs and then the appearance of the larvae is always within, let's say, seven days to a week to seven days to ten days, more or less, in these conditions. Now, as I said, the flies arrive very fast. So you, for example, could be dead, get colonised by the flies, and be buried. And when you are unburied, you will be found with all these maggots. But that doesn't mean that you've been exposed for ten days to the surface. So it is a very tricky -- a very tricky thing, because the flies are very fast to get to you. So in those terms, and understanding that there were many people in one single hole and not just one single body, I would say the state of preservation of the bodies in general was the same -- within the same site. It is not as if we have found, for example, I don't know, 20 bodies totally preserved and one totally skeletonised, that you would say, Well, this is not, I mean, explainable. But what were you finding? That you find all these people and in the centre of that you have one body that's totally skeletonised, then you would say, Well, perhaps this body's older or came from somewhere else. This was not the case. So the state of preservation or decomposition of the remains was -- per site was quite consistent within itself. Okay? So that would be the explanation I could get to you. So you've got, for example, larval stage of colonisation of flies and equal, let's say, decomposition regarding that, but obviously having many bodies in a -- in a -- in a single hole also will recreate a microenvironment that will tend either to preserve or decay the bodies at the same rate within the same assemblage, so to speak. I don't know whether I'm answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Up to a part in terms of the time of burial. However, Dr. Baraybar, let's now just stick to July, the second and the third week of July. Can we -- or were you able to tell whether that person was killed on the 10th, the 11th, the 12th, the 13th, or was that on the 14th or the 15th or the 16th, or was it something that happened after the 16th actually? This is why I'm asking you this. We have no evidence about reprisals or illegal executions before the 14th and after the 16th, and we know that a large number of people were killed outside of the illegal executions.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, I tend to disagree [Realtime transcript read in error "agree"] with you. Obviously the pathology expert will discuss these issues regarding injuries, but I would give you my position regarding this. I think that one of the things we do is to determine the most probable cause of death. In other words, certainly you do not know, and you will never know, whether the person died of a heart attack when it saw the gun and -- and died and then you shot a dead body. That is actually immaterial. If we were assuming that, no investigation anywhere in the world could be done. I mean, pretty much whenever you have a skeletonised body you couldn't say much about it. I think that the logic is rather different. Meaning, is it the injury you are recording a lethal injury or not? Meaning, if someone gets shot on the head, this person dies or not. Therefore what you're determining is the most probable cause of death. Also given by the context in which other people have been found. In other words, going back to this context here, what is the likelihood of these people burying themselves and then having bullets fired through their bodies and lying under them in the soil is, I will say, improbable, to say the least. Yet again not impossible, but improbable. Therefore in this case what you are reconstructing is the most probable, not the most possible scenario. And as such you're determining also the most probable cause of death. Otherwise, unless you have, I mean, a cadaver, you wouldn't -- you wouldn't be able to say absolutely anything. So it is a very fair scientific assumption you have to take prior to undertaking any kind of work of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
