If the injuries on the body and the slugs are in the same area, in other words, they are consistent with each other, that would then mean that the shots were fired while the body were in that position, lying down.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. I don't want to get into a discussion here, but just for the sake of purism, what you're saying is correct. We could envisage other certainly more complicated scenarios, but in general terms it is correct. If you have -- but it depends on a number of factors, certainly. I mean, you can have -- talking about all the infinite possibilities, that, for example, somebody shooting a standing person from above and as such the bullet will tend to come back to the ground, but then you would need to measure the distance and the height by which this person is shooting somebody from above to below first to the head and see it's like a triangle, to see where trajectory ends on the ground, and perhaps this will be much bigger that the extension that the grave has. Therefore, it is highly probable, most likely, that the people were indeed lying down and that is why you found the slugs under the head, the chest, and the pelvis. In an another scenario, I would concur with you that perhaps there are other explanations for it than people could have been standing or running or whatever, but in this case I would say it's quite straightforward that it is most likely that people were lying down in this hole, whatever, when they were shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since it is impossible to determine whether those injuries were inflicted while the people were still living, based on the strategic of the bullets that were found there we cannot really establish whether those were the bullets that killed these people; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Actually, no. It is not impossible to determine whether the injuries were inflicted while the people were still living based on the trajectory. The trajectory has nothing to do with whether people were alive or dead. Your question actually is pointing at a much more -- an almost philosophical, I mean, discussion, regarding whether based on a bone you can determine whether the person had their heart beating or their brain working when they were shot at. And I told you no, that is not possible. But what you are not inferring things based on this impossibility. That impossibility primarily stems from the fact that when you work with a cadaver, right, you are not only establishing the cause of death, you're also establishing the mechanism of death, the pathophysiological mechanism by which this person ended up being dead. But obviously, having a skeleton, you have no organs. Therefore, you have to rely on a number of other things, such as the context is one of them. So, for example, if you find somebody that did not bury himself or herself with hands tied behind their back, blindfolded, with a gunshot wound to the head, it is highly improbable that this was a case, for example, of suicide, or that this person just had an accidental death; therefore, the issue of mechanism of death in this case is useless. What you're trying to determine in this case is the most probable cause of death. And certainly, in terms of purism, it is an assumption, because you cannot say whether the person saw the gun and then had a fit and just died and then you shot a dead body. But that is not, I think, the issue you're trying to determine. It's whether likely, if somebody gets shot at, this person dies or doesn't die. And therefore, for example, if you get shot in the hand, it's different than if you get a shot in the head, you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC

So I do not see what is the relationship between somebody shot at in an empty hole with a handgun rather than some other kind of -- some other kind of weapon on top of the fact that this individual does not have any military paraphernalia in itself. So obviously we are speculating here, I mean, and it really -- it doesn't really matter what I think personally whether this person is a combatant or not. Based on the evidence alone, I cannot tell you that this person was a combatant because I could not identify him as a combatant in terms of what we -- how we define a combatant. That's another story. But, I mean, he's not somebody dressed in fatigues or something of the kind. And you got this hole that -- that was something else. When I say gun emplacement, it's because you even have one of these large shells that is smashed. So it's smashed by something very heavy. So most likely something heavy was inside. I don't know, a tank. I mean, some kind of -- something big that was firing these 30 millimetre rounds that were quite -- quite -- quite big. And then suddenly you find a body thrown in that hole. utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just to confirm what you asked me earlier about those three autopsy reports that were all disclosed on the 9th of July, 2009: I also wanted to put on the record the watch report by Mr. Mills that was talked about both yesterday and today is on our 65 ter list with number 2480, just in case Mr. Karadzic wants to refer to that at all.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree, Dr. Baraybar, when a soldier gets killed, whatever army he belongs to, they wouldn't bury his equipment, his kit, or his rifle together with the body?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I mean, I -- it's beyond my field of expertise, so I wouldn't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But right now in relation to Kasaba 7 where one man was found you said you couldn't say whether he was a soldier or not because his military equipment or weapons were not found with him. My position is that not a single person alive would bury the equipment and the weapons of a soldier together with him.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: What I refer to was primarily paraphernalia, starting with clothing and things of the kind. I presume, but that's a totally personal opinion, that you wouldn't bury somebody with a weapon. But that's not being an expert opinion, that's just a personal opinion. But, I mean, I was referring specifically to clothing and other items that would, I mean, make it look as if this person was a soldier, a combatant of some kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And would you agree that if somebody's running from an advancing force the first best thing they would do would be to change into civilian clothes, shed the uniform?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yet again it's not my field of expertise. I mean, I don't think my opinion is worth anything as an individual. As an expert, I have no opinion regarding that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. But you mentioned this a moment ago, so I have to clear things up. Should I then just disregard all such comments that you made?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I mean, what comments? I -- I mean, I'm reading the proceedings here, and I don't see any -- any discrepancy between the things I'm saying. But if you believe there is one, please point it out to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: No. I accept it's not your field of expertise, but it looked like it was because even before the break you said the person was not a combatant because there were no paraphernalia with him, no artefacts that would indicate that he was a soldier. That's why I said, If somebody, a soldier, is running from an enemy army that's advancing, the first thing they would do would be to change into civilian clothing.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: There are two points here. I mean, first, I never said it was or was not a combatant, because, I mean, what I said is that there was no paraphernalia or clothing or anything that made me think it was a soldier as such. I mean, whether a combatant is a soldier or could be somebody dressed in civilians clothes is another story and another field of discussion that I will not engage in. But if what you are asking me here is regarding whether somebody running from the enemy line is changing clothing, well that, I have no opinion regarding that, because, I mean -- or if you want to know my personal opinion, that I do not know, I mean, what is the value of it as an individual, I presume that if you're running away from the enemy line you have to have other clothing to get changed in the run, what is something ... quite a difficult exercise, I believe. I mean, changing your trousers and shirt and whatever to other clothing while you're running. But, anyway that's my personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Mr. Karadzic, I view this as a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you did conclude that in this grave-site, Glogova 5, and we discussed it before the break, that there were leaves and clay from a different site around the bodies. Is it then reasonable to assume that these bodies were brought from somewhere else and then buried in that grave? It is a primary grave-site for them, but it's not the location where they met their death or were executed.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You must be familiar with the obligation to sanitise the terrain after combat. The mortal remains of humans and animals have to be removed; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I don't know if it's an obligation. It is, I would call it, a customary -- I mean a customary practice in some -- in some countries. Not in all the countries anyway. Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the summary and in the conclusions, you say that -- which grave is it? It ends with Glogova 7. Glogova 2 and Glogova 7, you say that 19 bodies were found. And the exhumation was on the 18th and 19th of August. Two were around 7. In the case of eight bodies, the cause of death was not established, and the rest had been killed by gunshot.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: We look in the report of Glogova 2 from 1999 and 2001? Are you referring to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: It's the 2001 report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Exhibit P4033. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] ... before me. P45034, summary for Nova Kasaba and the rest. In my text, it's page 8, Exhumations in Eastern Bosnia, August to October. In Serbian, it's page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, maybe it's my confusion, but that's -- the 1999 report is the one with Nova Kasaba in it. Glogova 7 is in the second report. It's not in that one. So I'm not sure which report we're focusing on at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's just a reference to Glogova 7. It's P4034. It's only summary and conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, you found all sorts of tinned food and clothing there; correct? Three persons had bandaged wounds and tourniquets.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I'm trying to locate, I mean, the page you're talking about. Only one second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 8 December 1999, exhumation report on mass graves in Eastern Bosnia. My page 8, your page 7, 8, or 9. And it's the chapter "Summary and Conclusions." We have the English version on the screen. You can see it on the monitor, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yeah, that's Nova Kasaba 4, but you're talking about Glogova; right? Or you're talking about Nova Kasaba? Because that -- I'm a bit confused. What -- what site are you talking about, Glogova or Nova Kasaba?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the one on the screen now, but the previous page contains references to Glogova 2 and Glogova 7. That's why I mentioned it. We have it on the screen now. Have a look, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah. Yes, I have it here, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it reasonable to infer that these were combatants who before death had been bandaged and had tourniquets put on them?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, it would be fair to conclude that they were individuals that were wounded by gunshot wound prior to being killed. I mean, whether they were combatants or not, I do not know. Yet again, there was no evidence, as I said, of some kind of combatant attire, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As we agreed a moment ago, nobody's crazy to bury equipment and weapons with bodies, and we didn't even have any uniforms, if you remember. Our armies were popular armies. Most men did not have uniforms. Even if they did not get a chance to change, many went through the entire war in civilian clothing. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I didn't. But yet again that's information that I'm not privy to. So if I, as an expert, have to make a definition, I have to use some measurable, visible, objective elements. I mean, in this case, for example, somebody with camouflage fatigues or some other military or something used by armed forces or police of anything of the kind - because I have dealt with, as a matter of fact, with military casualties too in other contexts - not in this specific context in which you identify this person as a military personnel as what you were seeing was something that I wouldn't, as a civilian, wear, for example. But, I mean, in this case what I've said at the beginning, and I keep saying, is that there was no objective elements that allow me to make that judgement. I mean, you are making that judgement and you have the right to do so, but, I mean, I cannot, I mean, as an expert make that judgement. I can as an individual tell you what I think or not, but that is totally irrelevant, I mean, in this testimony, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, probably, from your viewpoint as anthropologist, this is not relevant for our forensic affairs. It is relevant. Further below you talk about tinned food, items of clothing, et cetera. Would that be an indication of preparations for some individual journey? They have all sorts of canned food.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm struggling to understand why you are asking -- putting such questions to the witness. Is witness able to answer such questions? I think you're coming to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, my main purpose is to establish whether those were prisoners of war liquidated by someone or they were fighting men attempting a breakthrough and getting killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's a perfectly legitimate subject for your submission, but there are certain extent of questions to be put to this witness as an expert. Please move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I should now like to call up this report that we received courtesy of Mr. Mitchell. The first one we received, case K3166B. Can we call up that document in e-court.

utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first one I got. It's a combined report, not the three other ones. It was easier for me to review.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us show the second page. Please check whether this is the one you want, Mr. Karadzic. Otherwise we'll --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not the right document. The first one we were given in hard copy before the three other ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll try to match with the e-court number. We'll try the next one.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] ERN X0042483. No. 483. 0042483.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Reid tells me it's the third number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- that ends in 52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 2408. 65 ter number is 2408. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this case, you performed an anthropological forensic expertise, and Mr. Clark did the pathology.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I do not know if me personally did, but, I mean, somebody did for sure, yeah. I would need to look at the -- the anthropology forms or the part of the -- of the report where it says who did the anthropology examination. But for your -- I mean, what you're stating is correct, even if I was not individually involved necessarily. I do not recall the case by number, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree that physical defects in cadavers that underwent skeletonisation, degradation, et cetera, do not necessarily indicate a cause of death?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I think we had this discussion before, and I told you that I did not agree with you. I think that we were discussing one -- before one of the breaks, I mean, regarding the most probable cause of death and all the rest of it. I think I already answered that -- that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look at the cause of death. Do we have a way of establishing that this defect in the chest was at the same time the cause of death, and do we need to have a description of putrescent changes for that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, as I said at the beginning, what you determine here is the most probable cause of death. But in addition to that, what you're looking at is a summary of the autopsy report. So there is an autopsy report that comes along that explains, I guess, in detail what were the findings, in case what was broken, that there was a piece of jacket of the bullet that was still found in soft tissues of the back, and things of that kind, and therefore it was the opinion of the pathologist in this case that the gunshot wound to the chest was the most probable cause of death in this specific case. We are not talking about pathophysiology of death and whether the person had a heart attack before being shot or something of the kind. That is totally immaterial in this discussion. But regarding what we're seeing on the screen, we're just looking at the summary yet again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to see this report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not me personally, but, I mean, if the Chamber wants, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we seat next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says the gender was determined through pathological analysis of soft tissues and pathologically it could not be established.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Anthropologically, no, it's not that it could not be established. It meant that whenever you had external genitalia present and a body was saponified or otherwise was visible, you wouldn't need to go through the effort of accessing, for example, the pelvic cavity in order to see whether it was really a male. If you're seeing genitalia there, it is, I mean, enough to determine the person is male or female, for that matter. If you have no genitalia, then you have to do the very invasive, I mean, work of going into the pelvic cavity first, skull later, and then long bones if it is the case in order to observe different characteristics. But if you have external genitalia, I mean, that's why you put indeterminant because you didn't take the effort, the extra effort, to just go and investigate those structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So anthropologically it was determined that the age was 35 and 60 and the height had a margin of error of 7.7?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: That is -- that is correct. But just for you to know, all the height determination in order to be -- or to be fit into a 95 per cent confidence interval will have the same standard deviation. What makes, as a matter of fact, and if I may, the estimation of stature pretty much useless in many contexts, because at the end of the day stature is as a legal -- with a legal value, is a stature that may be on a piece of personal ID. And if you are a tall person and you report yourself as shorter, or if you're short and report yourself as taller, what is on your ID is what is valid. Not your real stature. So this is really an academic discussion that can go on and. But just for the record, to understand that this type of estimation here is not, let's say, unique to this kind of work, it is as broad and as general as in any other kind of setting. You always will have a plus/minus 5, plus/minus 7 centimetres, what makes quite -- I mean, determination quite useless in many respects.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see page 3. Sorry, 3 pages further. It's the autopsy report. This was the summary, and we want the report now. It says the ERN ends in 486.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it's safe -- it's fair to the witness to seat next page and then move on to the autopsy report. Albeit briefly. Next page. Very well. Let's move on to the page Mr. Karadzic indicated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It has to be one page before. [In English] Other page for autopsy report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is a description of a complete body with some soft tissue, fragments of skin, clothing, ligature around the wrists made of cloth. Can we see the degree of putrefaction changes here that enable us to establish the time of death?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: As I said at the beginning, such determination in the conditions in which we have worked and in the condition in which the bodies were buried makes it, I mean, senseless. As I said at the beginning, we are not dealing with fresh cadavers here where you have very specific signs that may allow you to calculate a post-mortem interval. Therefore, the examinations at naked eye, as it is this case, of a body alone as the body alone will not allow you to say whether this body -- when this person died and became a body at, you know, a specific time or day. Obviously it is -- it would be safe to say or accurate to say that these people did not die 50 years before, but certainly you can't say otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baraybar. You can ask the same question with respect to ten -- for example, 1.000 bodies. I think it's -- I find it to be repetitive. Come to a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I have to move on to something else, but I have to draw the conclusion that even if I were a pathologist, I could not do more than you have done. I cannot establishment time of death; right?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: The time of death, certainly not. Nor you nor anybody else. The time of death, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How accurately? What is the time range, 50 years?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. What I said is that you will not be enable to say, based on what we have found, that these people belonged to, I mean, some outrageous interval of time, 50 years, a hundred years, or so on, because there were obviously elements to say they were contemporaneous remains. Right? I mean, that is what we have said at the beginning as well. I mean, the conditions which they were buried; they were saponified; some of them, depending on the soil conditions, some of the them skeletonized, et cetera. However, I also have said, and I want to say for the last time, the condition of remains alone is not to be taken out of context. We have to take the context as a whole. And the context as a whole means that you have bodies, you've got artefacts associate to those bodies, you've got all sorts of other things that allow you to pinpoint some kind of interval. You've got ID cards, you've got watches, you've got all sorts of things, and all those things together and independently point out to the same time interval. So I do not think it is correct to assume or to try to insinuate that we are looking at bodies that are naked and in a hole. And we have, with the naked eye again, to make an estimate, that would be a guesstimate, as a matter of fact, of when they died. I think that there has been explained sufficiently that we are not looking at things separately. So we have to look at things in context. And as an archaeologist, when I was in the field, I was recovering a context. I was not recovering bodies and then dropping everything else. I was not taking a body out and then getting the clothes out and just throw it on the side and the watches or whatever. All this evidence together is what allowed me to express expert opinions regarding different things such as the ones that I presented in these reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we just briefly see the second page to confirm that a razor was found, cigarettes, a lighter, two keys were found on this body. Can we say page 2 of the document. Yes, it's written there, but it's also written in the summary. Is that right? I am particularly interested in the razor. This was recorded; correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. Whatever you see there was recorded, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I won't be asking you whether you know that a prisoner would not be allowed to keep a razor.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Is that a question or a statement? I mean, you asked me if I know. Well, I understand that a prisoner in a prison is not allowed to have a razor, a gun, anything of the kind, in a prison. Yes, that is my understanding, I think. I'm not a prison expert either, but it would be my understanding that people in a prison or confined in a cell would not be allowed to have something with which it can hurt himself or some other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were speaking about the minimal number. Do you know the findings of Mr. Manning, who determined that DNA analysis established 5.021 and there were certain overlaps so it had to be reduced to 4.017 in total?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, I was not aware of that report. I mean, I have not read Mr. Manning's report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You said Mr. Manning's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes. Citation please, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the 65 ter number, but in the B/C/S it's 0614-8656, and then 8680. And then on the next page of the summary of the forensic material of 2007, Mr. Manning says -- if we can see that on the screen, that would be even better. ERN number in the B/C/S is 0614.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Baraybar didn't know about Dean Manning's report. There's no point of putting that. What is your question for this witness, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps Dr. Baraybar does not know about these findings, but he knows about the minimum number. That's what he was working on. Also Mr. Manning was working on that in 2007 after Dr. Baraybar dealt with that. So actually this then amounts to new information. And I thought it would be all right to show that to the witness. 65 ter 3936. It's the second page. Yes, just one moment, please. I don't have that. Yes, yes. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since you did look at the minimum number, I would like you to look at the second paragraph, where the responsibility for the exhumation of mass graves is discussed, that this was transferred to the Government of Bosnia and Herzegovina from the ICTY, and then it states all victims identified through the DNA analysis at the ICMP is 5021.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up a little bit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The other way round, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look and can you see whether it states there that 758 unique DNA records were found which had not been matched to a person yet? They don't know whose samples they are, so that number should be subtracted from the total. And then can we -- yes, yes, on the next one we see what was it that was done. Victims relating to Srebrenica that were identified --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat what you said. Interpreters couldn't follow.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You can see it on the screen. Srebrenica victims are identified via DNA analysis in mass graves, 4.017.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Baraybar, do you agree that the DNA, if it's accurate, cannot be disputed in any way? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, everything can be disputed in anyway, even DNA. But, I mean, in this case, I guess, in the context of your question I would say, I mean, I agree with you, yeah, it cannot be disputed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we look at the next page, please. Well, all right. We don't have to deal with this any more. All right. Thank you. Thank you for the answer and I hope I will have the opportunity to discuss this document with the author. Do you agree that in all of these findings the time of death and the time of burial were not established either through forensic or anthropological examination?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. As I've said many times, yes, you're correct. Not through anthropological examination. Not through the naked-eye examination or remains, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I just ask for a moment, please. Dr. Baraybar, do you know who Dusan Janc is?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No. Doesn't -- I mean, doesn't ring a bell by name, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think that he's one of the investigators of the OTP. In 2009, already, you didn't have any insight into the materials that became available in 2009; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Yes. And remember that I left ICTY in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the D number. This has been admitted. Can we show Dr. Baraybar 65 ter 21024. D1975. Yes. MR. KARADZIC [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at this piece at the bottom, 12 individuals. But you can look at the whole document as well, where you can see the need for certain persons to be excluded from certain localities. I don't need to read that to you. You can just look at that for yourself, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: You're referring to the paragraph number 3, 12 of individuals, that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Can you -- regarding Kravica.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, and you can see that at the bottom, "Nevertheless ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll up a little bit please. [In English] "Nevertheless considering ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let him read out the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I read it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. What is your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This information from 2009, does that complicate even further the precision and the accuracy of the data?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This is a hard copy that may assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I -- I took his word that he read it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, if he -- would you like to have the hard copy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, that's fine. I mean, that's fine. The -- I mean, I don't -- I cannot really give you an opinion whether it complicates matters or not. I mean, obviously I'm presented with a report that I do not know is part of what -- or anything. So I'm just seeing a number here, and it says that some people came from Kravica and that is part of investigation, but I think we are combining apples and potatoes here. I mean, they're two different sorts of data. I do not -- I mean, I -- what I would need to do for -- to give you an opinion would be to examine this document and whatever other documents that are being used to prepare this document and compare it with my own documents and tell you whether it complicates matter or not. But, I mean, for the time being, I -- this in 2009, the last report here 2004, so I cannot tell you much more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, Mr. Janc is coming as witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I wanted to ask Dr. Baraybar, in view of the fact that information evolves, does that mean that the information from the time when you made your conclusions was not definitive?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: No, of course. Of course it was not definitive. Imagine the -- if you look through the reports of minimal number, it was changing from 800 -- 1.800 something to two thousand and something and then it went back, and I expect of course that further work has been done. As in the previous report it was said by Manning that exhumations were handed over to the local Bosnian authorities therefore more graves would be exhumed. DNA results will always be higher than the minimal number of individuals, that it is minimal. And then I presume that perhaps the working figure now is much higher than the one we worked at the time. But I have never suggested that my reports were definitive. Imagine. I mean, these reports date from almost ten years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And do you agree that these additional data by Dr. Janc indicates that some graves were filled later? Not only were some robbed, but some were added to later. If it's easier for you to answer after looking at a hard copy, then I would kindly ask Mr. Mitchell to show it to you.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: I can receive a hard copy, and I will take, I mean, some time, I guess, to review it. But, I mean, I don't want to give you an answer regarding something I'm not privy too and just on the examination of a page of a document. I would be -- as far as a scientist, of course, I would like to see these corrigendum to begin with. So it is the corrigendum of something I do not have with me. So in order to give you actually an opinion, I would like to see, for that matter, what is the original document. If the Chamber allows it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Fair enough. I will now ask you to come to -- to conclude, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Dr. Baraybar, you were very kind and you met with the Defence. We talked, among other things, about some conventions and some good customs and even the obligations of the interested parties, parties that are interested in investigations. You confirmed that the UNHCR promulgated a sort of guide for good practices in the analysis of mortal remains, and you know that there is such a practice. The UNHCR did that in 1991, as you said, and this was done also by the UNMIK in Serbia, Serbian UNMIK in Kosovo exchanged experts and expert reports, and they allowed each other access and access to all the interested parties; is that right? Can you briefly tell the Trial Chamber what practice was introduced if you're not in a position to name the document, at least, that regulates that?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Just to clarify what I -- what we discussed yesterday in the meeting we had, we referred to two sets of documents. The first one is the Minnesota Protocol. The Minnesota Protocol published, as a matter of fact, by the High Commissioner of human rights of the UN in 1991. That it is a guide. It's not a covenant. It's just a guide of best practices to the investigation of human rights violations primarily committed by states against their own citizens. And recommending the impartiality and the fact that it should be an independent body the one investigating those crimes. It has another section regarding the treatment or the examination of remains as well as the exhumation of remains that are the way you should proceed in autopsy, if there's a suspicion of -- of torture, how you should examine the body, meaning a fresh body, and also skeletal remains. So that is a recommendation of best practice. I would say, personally, that the way we worked collectively throughout all these years fulfilled completely what is recommended in the Minnesota Protocol. Since there's no covenant that I know of, but I'm no lawyer either, I'm just telling you pretty much commonsensical answers, the documents I quoted, and now I can correct, because I -- yesterday I think I told you four, but there are actually three. There were three memorandums of understanding that were signed between UNMIK and the Serb government regarding the exchange of experts and expertise, joint parties to look for hidden prisons, and repatriation of remains. I believe Professor Dunjic, as well, is quite versed on -- on -- on those protocols because they were applied at the time I was in Kosovo, as a matter of fact, to facilitate repatriation of the remains from the mass graves in Batajnica, Petrovo Selo, and so on, into Kosovo, and the remains of Kosovo Albanian, Kosovo Serb victims into Serbia proper. So these are the two sets of documents we discussed yesterday, and I know of as -- that exist, but there's no other protocol I know of that regulates or imposes or demands any other kind of exchange of -- of anything, I mean, or witness of one party to be in the other one. I mean, that is -- I mean, that is -- as I said even the one in UNMIK was an MOU, memorandums of understanding. It was not even a covenant of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But today, just now, you have said that it's desirable and customary for the investigations to be carried out by an independent body. Do you agree that interested parties do have some right at least to observe the investigations and the examinations in order to be able to recognise them or acknowledge them as legitimate?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Minor correction: I didn't say that. What I said is the Minnesota Protocol, not me, requests or suggests or recommends, whenever state -- the state may be involved in killings on citizens, for independent commission to be set up. So it is not, I mean, quite the same thing. And remember, the Minnesota Protocol was primarily created or influenced, very much influenced by Latin American states killing and disappearing its own citizens. So it's a very specific thing now. Obviously now it's a broad recommendation, and even -- there is even another protocol regarding the examination of remains, that it's been put forward through the High Commissioner for human rights again, and there's another legal protocol on the treatment of -- of the dead produced by the ICRC, but all these are like recommendations of best practices. There's no covenant of any kind, I mean, enforcing or anything, anybody, to do anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now your last question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And do you agree that it would be very useful and it would make the recognition of the reports much easier had the Serbian side had access at least to the investigations conducted by the Bosnian government as a party that cannot be called a disinterested party, as well as the investigations that were carried out by the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Here again, I mean, I may have a personal opinion. But, I mean, as an expert I have no expert opinion regarding that. I mean, yet again, I mean, it would be a very subjective opinion, the one I have. I mean, whether I agree or don't agree as a person, it is immaterial to my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, go ahead and give us your subjective opinion. If that's the only instance of you putting forward a subjective opinion, then the Defence will accept that.

utterances.speaker: JOSE PABLO BARAYBAR
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the -- the results of any -- of any investigation that is contested, I mean, should be shared whenever possible with all the interested parties. I mean, that's, for me, a commonsensical thing. The problem is that when you have a contested subject, no matter what, even if the results are made public or shared with the parties, I mean, the parties will tend to keep the opinion they had at the beginning, no matter what. Even if the evidence is there. So that's something -- that's regrettably something else that I have seen throughout my career. But I'm all for transparency in any kind of setting, in any country, in any conflict, in anything. That's -- that's my own personal opinion.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Baraybar, I would like to thank you very much both for meeting with the Defence and also for your testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Baraybar. On behalf of this Chamber and the Tribunal as a whole I would like to thank you for coming yet again to The Hague to give it. Now you're free to go. But we'll rise all together. Unless there's any further matters to be raised, we'll adjourn for the week. And we'll resume next week at 9.00 on Monday with Dr. Riedlmayer. Have a nice weekend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 5th day of December, 2011, at 9.00 a.m.
